summary:
Nemotron-TwoTower: Diffusion Language Modeling with Pretrained Autoregressive Context
"We propose TwoTower, a block-wise autoregressive diffusion model that decouples these roles into two towers: a frozen AR context tower that causally processes clean tokens, and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the context."
"Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while offering 2.42X higher wall-clock generation throughput."
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuYfCSbgAAMDss.jpg
clean_summary:
Nemotron-TwoTower is a diffusion language model that separates the roles of context processing and denoising into two towers. The autoregressive context tower processes clean tokens causally and is frozen, while the diffusion denoiser tower uses bidirectional block attention and cross-attention to refine noisy blocks.

The model retains 98.7% of the quality of a traditional autoregressive baseline while achieving 2.42 times higher generation throughput in wall-clock time.

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
clean_title: Open-sourcing AI evaluation frameworks enables reproducibility and progress tracking
summary:
i completely agree about the importance of having AI evaluation frameworks open-sourced so they can be periodically run with the latest models...
this is EXACTLY the motivation behind why we developed Medmarks!
Quoting @yishan
A big problem with research studies on AI models is that given how long the peer review process is, the results are always out-of-date by the time the paper is published.
This time, we have something better!
The typical reaction to research results like this roughly goes "You're just testing on old models. Today's models are way better and surely can do it now!"
But the best solution is for these papers to also open-source all of their testing framework so that upon publication, others can reproduce their results, as well as run it on the newest models of the day - and into the future. After all, "this is the worst they'll ever be" so what really matters is determining when they DO pass the threshold.
As it turns out, the authors of this paper DID open-source their evaluation framework!
Here:
So I figured... let's re-run the tests on the latest models!
Summary of our results are here:
One drawback is that, unfortunately, the authors didn't (or weren't legally able to) open-source ALL the testing data, since apparently some of it is copyrighted by JAMA/NEJM etc. That's a separate problem with the medical research publishing industry for another time.
However, we were able to reproduce the test on the public datasets they did include!
First, we re-ran the same tests (as closely as we could) on the old models the paper claimed to use, in order to establish a baseline and determine how much "drift" there would be. (Answer: not too much)
Then we ran those tests on the newest frontier models we could find.
The results are: the most capable models today (GPT-5.5 Pro) did outperform the best models from before (79/100 vs 69/100), but did not improve enough to be considered sufficient for reliable medical use.
In fact, the paper's criterion for "fit for reliable medical use" is more stringent, requiring the models to be robust under perturbation and bad data, knowing when to say there's not enough information, give clinically valid reasoning rather than hallucinations, etc. Those sound pretty reasonable to me.
I wasn't able to reproduce that kind of qualitative evaluation, but even on the basic pass/fail test using public datasets of interpreting radiology images, the newest models are better, but not yet quite good enough.
Nevertheless, I would like to praise the paper's authors for at least open-sourcing what they could, enabling me to (fairly quickly) attempt to reproduce their results. This is definitely a step in the right direction!
While my reproduction wasn't able to be comprehensive, it certainly gave me useful directional info and - perhaps more importantly - allowed me (a random dude on the internet) to directly reproduce the results in their paper and validate them.
I would like to encourage ALL authors of research papers on AI models to do similar open-sourcing of their experimental frameworks!
clean_summary:
i completely agree about the importance of having AI evaluation frameworks open-sourced so they can be periodically run with the latest models. This motivation led to the development of Medmarks, which allows others to reproduce results and test new models.

A researcher highlights that many research studies on AI models become outdated quickly due to long peer review processes. To address this, the paper's authors open-sourced their evaluation framework, enabling others to re-run tests on the latest models. Reproducing the tests on older models established a baseline, and running them on newer models showed some improvement, but not enough for reliable medical use, especially under real-world conditions.

The effort demonstrates that open-sourcing evaluation tools is a valuable step toward transparent, reproducible AI research. It allows independent validation, tracking progress over time, and encourages other researchers to share their frameworks, ultimately advancing the field.

summary:
What if instead of autoresearch reflecting incremental progress from a single person, it reflected *hundreds* of researchers’ progress, updated live, with every run’s data point being interactive and reproducible? You could survey the full space of explored ideas, see which changes actually move the benchmark, and fold the most promising ideas into your next run.
Labless ( is my attempt at this. It can support thousands of simultaneous training runs across contributors around the world, each learning & improving together to hillclimb on a fixed benchmark, validated using a standardized codebase scaffold.
Importantly, all valid training runs auto-submit to Labless, so failed experiments are as visible and reproducible as the successes. We have an agentic API that lets you or your coding agent study every run submitted so far so you don't waste time investigating something someone already tried, and you can source novel ideas from other contributors.
Labless already hosts our Nanopath challenge to build the best pathology foundation model that trains in 1 hour on a single GPU. We are hoping to expand the platform further and support a suite of open-source research challenges.
If this resonates with you, if you think the path to research innovation lies in open-source collaborative hill-climbing, please reach out.

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
summary:
SigLIP useful for mind-reading research? Check!
Quoting @iScienceLuvr
The Aligner uses a SigLIP contrastive loss to learn word-level alignment between the Encoder's MEG embeddings and the LLM's word embedding space.
Whenever the CTC path from the Encoder predicts a space, it chops up the continuous MEG into neural "words".
Because spaces are frequent (about 19% of characters) and robustly predicted, 86% of sentences have their word count estimated within ±1 word of the ground truth — which is what lets the LLM read the MEG as structured token input.

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
summary:
Can regularization based JEPA (e.g. SIGReg) scale and compete with SOTA foundation models (DINO)? Here is the answer: yes and with 10x less data.
VISReg (slight variation of SIGReg) competes with DINOv2-LVD142M while only training on inet22k.
Try it out:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMGJbemXgAARWrX.png
Quoting @HaiyuWu1
Working on world model or SSL? You definitely need to try our new work: VISReg!
What does it achieve?
💪 Strong collapse prevention: High gradient when embedding collapse
⚡ Friendly to scale training: Linear complexity to scaling factors
🧩 Easy to train: Similar to LeJEPA, it is a heuristic-free method
🏆 Best OOD performance: Achieving the best accuracy on 6 OOD datasets
📉 Data efficiency: Achieving a similar OOD average accuracy to DINOv2 with 90% less data
🧬 Robust to low-quality datasets: It is robust to long-tailed and sparse datasets
Our results also indicate that SIGReg type methods can scale up, filling in the missing piece in @ylecun's great talk
A big thanks to my co-author @randall_balestr and my manager @DrMorganLevine. Also, huge gratitude to @ylecun for connecting us to make this project happen! 🤝
#SelfSupervisedLearning #JEPA #WorldModel

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
clean_title: Deep dive into TPU and GPU cluster communication primitives
summary:
Immediately studying any one of Aleksa's blog posts will probably take you very very far...
Quoting @gordic_aleksa
New in-depth blog post time: "Inside TPU and GPU Clusters: The Anatomy of Collective Communication".
If you want to deeply understand the core primitives behind scaling the training / inference for MoEs and dense transformers, going a level below FSDP, expert parallelism, data parallelism, model/tensor parallelism this might be a fun read.
I cover:
* TPU cluster topology: (super)pods, slices, DCN, PCIe, ICI
* All-Gather: 1D/2D rings, and path algo (lots of visuals so should be crystal clear how these work even if you're not a perf engineer)
* Reduce-Scatter (which is the dual of AG) and All-Reduce
* All-to-All (used to dispatch tokens to target experts in MoEs)
* NVIDIA GPU cluster topology (reference DGX architecture): nodes, scalable units, fat tree
* GPU collectives within the node: rings, trees (log2 steps), and SHARP (in network compute unit)
* GPU collectives across nodes, hierarchical algorithms over InfiniBand
etc.
I was heavily inspired to do this deep dive after reading the excellent Scaling book by an excellent group of people @jacobaustin132 @_sholtodouglas @reinerpope and others!
What originally started as "let me maybe just make four figures covering All-Gather, Reduce-Scatter, All-Reduce, and All-to-All so I can understand them better, it shouldn't take more than a day, right, right?" somehow turned into this 40 figures later.
Along the way, I realized that the collective algorithms only really make sense once you understand the underlying hardware topology. TPUs were a bit easier to reason about, but I couldn't skip GPUs, I love them too much. Rings are cool, but I also wanted to understand tree algorithms. But also SHARP, and fat trees, and hierarchical collectives. :')
So the scope slowly expanded, and little by little, this blog post came to fruition. Just a side-quest.
Hope you like it! :)
---
Also a big thank you to my friends for reviewing the blog and providing feedback:
* @ArunDemeure (prev GPU/AI stuff at Magic, GPU architect at Apple and Imagine, my llm.c buddy!)
* @axel_s_feldmann (making GPUs go brrr at Jane Street, we met for the first time at @marksaroufim's excellent GPU mode event)
* @pranjalssh (ex xAI GPU wizard, one of two people who inspired my original matmul blog!)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNM6YzjbEAI_OSi.jpg
clean_summary:
Immediately studying Aleksa's blog post can provide a deep understanding of the core primitives behind scaling training and inference for MoEs and dense transformers, going beyond FSDP, expert parallelism, data parallelism, and model/tensor parallelism.

The post covers TPU cluster topology, All-Gather algorithms, Reduce-Scatter, All-Reduce, All-to-All communication used in MoEs, NVIDIA GPU cluster architecture, intra-node GPU collectives like rings and trees, and hierarchical algorithms over InfiniBand. It emphasizes that understanding hardware topology is essential to grasp collective algorithms, with detailed visuals and explanations of various algorithms and architectures.

The author was inspired by the Scaling book and expanded a small initial effort into a comprehensive resource with 40 figures, aiming to clarify complex communication patterns across hardware types. The post is a side-quest driven by a passion for understanding the hardware foundations of large-scale AI training.

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
clean_title: Debunking claims about Kimi K3's memory efficiency and DRAM demand
summary:
This take makes no sense to me. At the very least there is not enough evidence to back it up.
Let me explain:
1. Kimi K3 is the largest open-source model. It's 2.8T parameters, so that means the raw weights with quantization takes up 1.5 TERABYTES. You need an entire multi-node cluster to run this model (you're not running this on your laptop lol). Obviously this requires MORE DRAM than any previous open source model, not less!
2. What about the KDA? First of all, linear attention is nothing new (which to be fair is acknowledged in the post/clip) and Kimi K3 still uses some amount of regular attention as well. It is true that the model uses less DRAM per token and scales better as context size increases. However it doesn't solve the problem of needing a lot of DRAM for the model overall.
3. Even if it were true that Kimi K3 significantly reduces DRAM usage, it doesn't necessarily mean that the demand of DRAM would go down. Once again, people forget about Jevon's paradox!!
One example of why his conclusion is probably false: Kimi K3 had to pause subscriptions because they didn't have enough compute to support demand! I think it's clearly very easy to justify spending 500k on a new rack!
This is just the same story as when people were shorting NVIDIA when DeepSeek came out cuz it was more efficient. Since then GPU demand and NVIDIA market cap has just continued to grow lol
Quoting @kai_xbt
Bubble Boi reveals the Kimi breakthrough that made him sell his entire portfolio overnight
"Kimi is using a technique called linear attention that cuts down memory growth entirely to a fixed size, and they didn't just get okay results, they got world-class results. This same technique was used by the Qwen models but nobody thought it would scale. It's looking more and more likely that it scales pretty well, and if that's the case the memory per user is always fixed."
"So if every frontier model goes to this, the demand for DRAM drops significantly. They already bought the memory, they just serve more and more users. It's like you had a car and someone found a way to make it 10 times faster, you're not going to buy a new car."
"But you also have to readjust the assumption that hyperscalers are going to crazily spend for the next two years. What's to say there's not another innovation that shrinks this more and now you go from serving a thousand users to a hundred thousand users on one server rack? How do you justify spending 500k on a new rack at that point?"
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2080762177389203456/img/pTg5CbgVlwObQ9m2.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2080762177389203456/vid/avc1/480x270/9-UNGQqZ_JYqCXx5.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary: This take questions the assertion that Kimi K3 significantly reduces DRAM usage. Kimi K3 is the largest open-source model at 2.8 trillion parameters, requiring a multi-node cluster and over 1.5 terabytes of raw weights, which demands more DRAM than previous models. While it uses linear attention to scale better with context size, it doesn't eliminate the overall need for large amounts of DRAM. The argument that DRAM demand would decrease overlooks Jevon's paradox, where increased efficiency can lead to higher overall demand. For example, Kimi K3 had to pause subscriptions due to insufficient compute capacity, and the demand for GPUs and market cap for companies like NVIDIA has continued to grow despite efficiency improvements. Quoting @kai_xbt, the technique of linear attention may fix memory growth per user, enabling more users on the same hardware, but this doesn't necessarily mean DRAM demand will drop; it could just mean serving more users with existing memory. The idea that future innovations could further shrink resource needs and increase user capacity raises questions about the sustainability of current hardware spending.

clean_title: A comprehensive list of medical AI benchmarks including Medmarks
summary:
A good list of medical AI benchmarks, including @SophontAI's very own Medmarks suite :)
Quoting @pri_the_ninja
Current map of medical AI benchmarks:
🧠 CLINICAL JUDGMENT
• SCT-Bench tests whether models revise clinical judgments appropriately as uncertain evidence changes.
• CPC-Bench tests complex diagnosis, next-test selection and medical-evidence retrieval.
• Sequential Diagnosis tests whether models ask the right questions and order the right tests before reaching a diagnosis.
These capabilities are increasingly consolidated through MAST, which currently includes CPC-Bench and several benchmarks below. @drethangoh @vishnuravi @pranavrajpurkar @StanfordMed @harvardmed
🛡️ SAFETY + COMMUNICATION
• First Do NOHARM v2 tests whether models avoid harmful recommendations and critical omissions in clinical management.
• The HealthBench family, including HealthBench Professional which is where the graph is from, tests realistic patient and clinician conversations using case-specific physician rubrics. @OpenAI @thekaransinghal
• MedRiskEval, including PatientSafetyBench, tests patient-facing risks such as unsafe advice, misinformation, overconfidence and bias. @MSFTResearch
👁️ MULTIMODAL REASONING
• ReXrank Mini tests interpretation and report generation from radiology images. @pranavrajpurkar
• IMCBench tests safe, accurate reasoning in image-grounded, multi-turn medical conversations. @AmazonScience
• AgentClinic tests clinical agents that must interact with patients, collect multimodal information and use tools. @npjDigitalMed
🧰 EHR + AGENTIC CARE
• MedAgentBench v2 tests whether agents can retrieve information and complete actions inside a FHIR-based EHR. @AndrewYNg @james_y_zou @NEJM_AI
• PhysicianBench tests long-horizon physician tasks grounded in longitudinal patient records.
• LongMedBench tests memory and temporal reasoning across repeated visits and evolving treatment.
• EHR-Complex tests executable reasoning over real clinical databases.
🏥 BROAD CLINICAL WORKFLOWS
• MedHELM tests clinical decisions, documentation, patient communication, research and administration. @StanfordHAI @StanfordMed @NatureMedicine
• MedMarks provides an open benchmark suite spanning medical reasoning, calculations, information extraction and EHR tasks.
I’m sure I missed some, lmk what to add!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOj5G2yXcAAWbHV.jpg
clean_summary: This tweet shares a detailed list of benchmarks used to evaluate medical AI systems. It covers areas such as clinical judgment, safety and communication, multimodal reasoning, electronic health record (EHR) interactions, and broad clinical workflows. For example, SCT-Bench tests how models revise judgments with uncertain evidence, while CPC-Bench evaluates complex diagnosis and evidence retrieval. Safety benchmarks like First Do NOHARM v2 assess harmful recommendations, and MedRiskEval evaluates risks like misinformation. Multimodal reasoning benchmarks include ReXrank Mini for radiology interpretation and IMCBench for medical conversations grounded in images. EHR-related benchmarks test information retrieval, long-term reasoning, and complex reasoning over clinical databases. The list highlights ongoing efforts to create comprehensive evaluation suites for medical AI, with some benchmarks like MedMarks spanning multiple tasks. The author invites suggestions for additional benchmarks.

title: Tanishq Mathew Abraham, Ph.D. (@iScienceLuvr)
clean_title: Child prodigies in biology and the role of data and encouragement
summary:
Fun fact: my initial research interest was focused on synthetic biology and drug delivery. I have a background in synthesizing cell-free systems and synthetic cells.
Unfortunately the lab I was working in did not have funding to keep me, so after exploring different options I moved to medical AI.
I was also highly interested in a variety of other fields in bio, for example, immunology. I remember at the age of ~11 years old reading Janeway's Immunbiology from start to finish over the course of a few months and exploring some research ideas
which I shared with an immunologist who was impressed and said they were graduate-level ideas.
Now I work on medical AI which isn't medicine per se but definitely my bio background has been extremely useful for me as a scientist.
So yeah I don't think there's any inherent limitation for why there can't be child prodigies in biology. Perhaps it's just something that's not encouraged as much.
Part of it could be the idea that having a young kid in a lab is a recipe for disaster. Going through college I indeed received a lot of pushback for trying to complete some of the basic labs aand I had to repeatedly prove myself over and over again.
If you encourage kids to accelerate in theoretical and computational areas for the sake of "safety" then such an outcome is not surprising at all. It does not mean the children aren't capable though.
Quoting @SynBio1
Why are there no child prodigies in biology?
This question seems to me to reveal something important about the nature of biological knowledge
It has new relevance as try to distinguish questions that can be answered with pure intelligence from those that require large datasets
clean_summary: The author shares their background in synthetic biology, drug delivery, and immunology, highlighting that early interest and encouragement can foster prodigious talent in biology. They note that societal perceptions and safety concerns often hinder young children from pursuing lab work, despite their capabilities. The discussion emphasizes that biological knowledge increasingly depends on large datasets, which influences how we recognize and support young talent in the field.

clean_title: Drug discovery and AI's role in understanding human biology
summary:
"Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands" - a great blog post by Daphne Koller, a pioneer in the space of AI for drug discovery!
A few of my thoughts:
- Koller makes an important point that a major limiting factor is relating biological mechanisms to human clinical outcomes. It's something we think a lot about at @SophontAI. Our belief is that foundation models trained on clinical data will serve as useful "instruments" that can help tackle this problem: interpretability on foundation models will allow us to at least generate biologically relevant and testable hypotheses of clinical mechanisms.
- Koller talks about how the biggest impact AI can have on the drug-to-patient phase (since it connects to the disease biology directly) is "selecting the patients most likely to respond, confirming that the drug is hitting its intended target, and detecting early and reliable signals that it is actually modifying disease biology." Once again, we believe clinical foundation models can help out a lot here!
- The same "elephant and blind scientists" parable is mentioned as we do in our @SophontAI launch announcement, although with a slightly different context
The idea is very simple: in order to understand how to best cure a disease, you need to understand disease biology in humans directly. AI foundation models should therefore be trained directly on human data! That's what we focus on!
I have written a little bit about some of this on Twitter already:
Quoting @a16z
The data we need to understand human biology is about 1000x the quantity we've collected
Full piece from @insitro founder and CEO @DaphneKoller:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOzvaRibIAAYeOj.jpg
clean_summary: A blog post by Daphne Koller highlights that drug discovery lacks simple solutions and emphasizes the challenge of relating biological mechanisms to clinical outcomes. Foundation models trained on clinical data could help generate biologically relevant hypotheses and improve patient selection, target confirmation, and early disease signals detection. The idea is that AI models should be trained directly on human data to better understand disease biology, which is a focus at @SophontAI. Koller also notes that understanding human biology requires vastly more data than currently collected, about 1000 times more, to enable transformative medicine breakthroughs.

clean_title: Benchmarking 32 foundation models on pathology tasks reveals performance insights
summary:
A recent study by Stanford researchers benchmarked 32 foundation models on a diverse suite of 41 pathology tasks!!
Here's what they found:
1. Pathology-specific vision models (Path-VM) outperform pathology-specific vision-language models (Path-VLM). Perhaps this reflects that there are still limitations in multimodal architectures
2. Scaling model size and training data does not uniformly improve pathology model performance. This is exactly what we've observing too!
3. Model ensembling improves task performance. Ensembling the top 5 models achieved the highest mean accuracy when aggregated over 19 tasks.
The best individual models on the benchmark suite include Virchow2 (Microsoft), UNI (Harvard), H-Optimus-0 (Bioptimus), and Prov-GigaPath (Microsoft)
Paper link:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPPQ0libUAAxu8y.jpg
clean_summary: A recent study by Stanford researchers evaluated 32 foundation models across 41 pathology tasks. They found that pathology-specific vision models outperform vision-language models, possibly due to limitations in multimodal architectures. Increasing model size and training data does not always lead to better performance, aligning with observations in the field. Model ensembling, especially combining the top five models, improves accuracy, with Virchow2, UNI, H-Optimus-0, and Prov-GigaPath emerging as top performers. These findings highlight the importance of model specialization and ensemble methods in pathology AI.
